item.title: The "cabbage revolution" -- How China is using science to feed 1.4 billion people
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-17
WUHAN, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- There is nothing remarkable about the tiny cabbage seedlings growing in the fields of Jiayu County in central China. They are barely more than rows of green tufts against the soil, too young to look anything like the firm heads that will eventually find their way onto dinner tables across the country. Yet these modest plants tell the story of a decades-long scientific effort to develop better seeds, breed tougher varieties and make one of China's most ordinary vegetables more productive and reliable. Known as China's "cabbage UN" for its vast collection of varieties, Jiayu in Hubei Province has become a major hub for cabbage breeding, testing and production. The effort goes back to the 1980s, when China still relied on cabbage seeds imported from countries including Japan and the Netherlands. "We were determined to build our own capacity and take food production into our own hands," said Qiu Zhengming, chief scientist with the Hubei Academy of Agricultural Sciences, who works at a vegetable science and technology demonstration park in Jiayu. Led by pioneers, including Fang Zhiyuan of the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences, generations of researchers set out to find a way to ensure that people in China could have fresh, high-quality cabbage throughout the year. They started with the seed. Scientists developed China's first cabbage hybrid, followed by disease-resistant varieties and strains suited to different growing seasons. For winter harvests, they bred varieties that could withstand the cold while producing sweeter heads. The results have accumulated over decades. Today, more than 70 percent of winter cabbage grown in China's major winter-cabbage producing areas comes from domestic varieties, according to researchers. "Using science and technology to improve production is important," Qiu said. "Once you have that foundation, farmers' incomes become more stable." At Jiayu's 460-mu (about 31-hectare) vegetable science and technology demonstration park, researchers test more than 2,000 cabbage varieties each year, continually introducing and screening new ones to find those best suited to local conditions. The experiments go beyond cabbage. Researchers are also developing new varieties of vegetables that are staples on Chinese dinner tables, including winter melon, pumpkin and Chinese cabbage. Modern breeding techniques, including hybrid breeding and genetic technologies, are being used to improve resistance to cold and disease and to increase levels of fiber, vitamins and minerals. A nearly 100-mu area has also been established for fully mechanized cabbage production trials. The fields themselves have become part of the experiment. At the demonstration park, a network of digital sensors monitors weather, temperature, soil conditions, pests and diseases, as well as water and fertilizer levels. When something goes wrong, an alert can be sent directly to a farmer's smartphone. Drones fly over the fields to monitor crop health. The shift is giving farmers more control over their fields. Instead of relying on unpredictable weather, they can make decisions based on data. Farmers can also order seeds directly from a researcher-managed seed bank, saving them the time and uncertainty of breeding their own varieties and helping them avoid losses caused by bad weather. Jiayu's vegetables now reach markets across the country, including Hong Kong, Shanghai and Guangzhou. About 75,000 local farmers are involved in vegetable cultivation and their incomes have increased. For farmer Liu Lianhong, the benefits are measured in more familiar terms. Her household income comes mainly from land-transfer payments and annual dividends from a vegetable farming company, while she also works there. These days, she is busy transplanting cabbage seedlings and clearing weeds. What is happening in Jiayu is part of a much larger effort in China to use agricultural science to strengthen domestic food supplies. Perhaps the best-known example is hybrid rice, pioneered by Yuan Longping. The breakthrough dramatically increased rice yields and helped China meet much of its own demand for rice. Hubei, a major grain-producing province, is now developing high-yield, high-protein corn as an alternative that could help reduce reliance on imported soybeans. Researchers are also breeding fish with improved meat quality. In neighboring Henan Province, scientists have developed rice varieties less prone to lodging. In Shaanxi Province, researchers have developed drought-tolerant, high-yield wheat. Some of these agricultural technologies and varieties have also traveled beyond China, helping farmers in Central Asia and Africa increase production and incomes. These efforts are about more than seeds, technology and yields. They are ultimately about people's lives. "Of all the things that matter, the well-being of people matters most," Qiu said. ■

item.title: A 3,000-year-old glimpse into China's Bronze Age technological prowess
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-17
WUHAN, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- China is famous for its ancient inventions: papermaking, printing, gunpowder and the compass. But there is far more to its technological legacy than these. One notable achievement is the Tonglushan ancient copper mining site. More than 3,000 years ago, people in China were already mining and refining high-purity copper on a large scale at this site, a feat that put them some 2,000 years ahead of the rest of the world. Located in Daye, Hubei Province in central China, this site has welcomed more than 20 million visitors since it opened in the 1980s, including tourists from Japan, the Republic of Korea, Europe and Africa. It received official designation as a National Archaeological Site Park in 2025 and is now working toward UNESCO World Heritage status. To further showcase China's ancient industrial achievements to international visitors, a large-screen presentation launched last year features English subtitles alongside Chinese ones, while the park has also opened an educational workshop for visitors from China and abroad. "The site shows that China has long had the capacity to develop advanced technologies independently. It also strengthens our cultural confidence," said Chen Jiayi, a staff member at the site park. In the 21st century, China has once again emerged as a major industrial and technological power -- home to the world's most comprehensive industrial systems and making rapid advances in areas ranging from new-energy vehicles and artificial intelligence to robotics, quantum technology, space exploration and marine science. The Tonglushan site was discovered by chance during mining operations in 1973, and archaeological excavations found that mining and smelting activity there dates back at least to the early years of the Spring and Autumn Period (770 B.C.-476 B.C.). "It confirms that China's Bronze Age civilization followed a complete and independent course of development," Chen said. "Archaeological comparisons show that the copper used in the Bianzhong of Marquis Yi of Zeng, a famous set of bronze chime bells, as well as many other bronze artifacts, came from Tonglushan." Excavations have found that the ancient mine shafts and tunnels at the site total more than 8,000 meters in length, and over 400,000 tonnes of smelting slag have been unearthed so far. Researchers estimate that between 80,000 and 120,000 tonnes of crude copper were produced there over the centuries, enough to cast about 48,000 sets of bronze bells comparable in scale to those of Marquis Yi of Zeng, or a far larger number of ritual vessels and weapons. "Bronze gave physical form to China's long-standing ritual and musical traditions, its social hierarchy, its way of life, and indeed its pluralistic yet unified civilization," Chen said. Ancient craftsmen at this location had already mastered sophisticated mining and smelting techniques. They used bellows-equipped shaft furnaces and two procedures, namely "oxidized ore to copper" and "sulphide ore to matte to copper," thereby precisely controlling furnace temperatures at around 1,200 degrees Celsius. At the time, crude copper reached a purity of 93 percent, while the copper content in slag was just 0.7 percent, which is a level far ahead of the rest of the ancient world, with some techniques approaching near-modern standards. Mining and metallurgical activity at Tonglushan never really stopped, and by the late 19th century it was home to what was then Asia's largest integrated iron and steel enterprise, while production further expanded after the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949. "Today, copper production here has moved into higher-value processing, serving fields such as new-energy vehicles, 5G communications and semiconductor chips," said Pan Xiaojin, mayor of Daye. Daye has also expanded into a range of other industries, including intelligent connected new-energy vehicles, optoelectronic information, hydrogen energy, intelligent robotics, the low-altitude economy and green building materials. "The spirit of craftsmanship, fueled by a drive to grow stronger and tempered through countless trials, continues to inspire us to create new wonders," Pan noted. ■

item.title: China's cycling boom pedals new wave of health-driven consumption
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-17
NANJING, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- For freshman Miao Xuan, the journey to university was more than just a trip to a new city. It was a 706-km bike ride that marked the beginning of a new chapter in his life. An outdoor sports enthusiast, Miao set off from east China's Fujian Province with his father, a cycling aficionado. Averaging about 70 km a day, the pair spent 10 days crossing three provinces before arriving in Nanjing, Jiangsu Province, where Miao was set to begin his university studies. "The trip was tiring, but cycling felt great," Miao said, adding that he plans to ride his bike to explore new cities whenever he gets the chance. "Cycling not only keeps me physically fit, but also refreshes my mind and helps improve my focus and perseverance." Thursday marks World Cycling Day. Before becoming the largest market and producer for automobiles, China was better known as the "kingdom of bicycles." Today, the country is still the largest maker of bikes anywhere in the world. Despite the rise of electric cars and the expansion of public transit networks, bicycles are still a go-to means of transport in China. In fact, bicycles have been enjoying something of a renaissance, with more young people embracing them as a fun way to get around and stay active. For cycling enthusiast Li Bin in Jiangsu's Wuxi, riding along the shores of Taihu Lake has become a regular ritual. Equipped with goggles, a helmet and other protective gear, he often speeds along the lakeside routes. "I started mainly to lose weight, and the results were quite noticeable. Gradually, I fell in love with the sport," said Li, who has been cycling for about two years. While shared bikes are everywhere in Chinese cities, more and more young people are choosing to buy their own bikes instead. For these cycling fans, owning a bike feels like an investment in a healthier lifestyle. "My first bicycle cost 2,500 yuan (about 370 U.S. dollars). I recently replaced it with another one, and after adding various accessories, the total cost came to around 10,000 yuan," Li said. An outdoor sports industry development report from the General Administration of Sport showed that China had more than 130 million cycling users as of August last year, while the output value of its bicycle industry reached 300 billion yuan. On Xiaohongshu, a Chinese lifestyle-sharing platform, cycling-related content has generated billions of views. At a bicycle store in Nanjing, rows of bikes in different designs and specifications line the showroom. "Consumers are no longer buying bikes based solely on appearance. They also care about the frame materials and overall design," said Zhang Lan, the store manager. Road bikes and mountain bikes priced between 2,000 yuan and 5,000 yuan are currently among the bestsellers, Zhang said. The store, which opened less than six months ago, has already generated more than 600,000 yuan in sales. Giant, a world-renowned high-end bicycle manufacturer, said it now operates more than 3,000 stores across China. The company has even launched a bike line just for women, with designs tailored to women's body shapes and aesthetic preferences, as female cycling participation and spending continue to rise. The range of cycling-related purchases is expanding beyond bicycles themselves to helmets, lights, cycling apparel, goggles, action cameras and other accessories, creating increasingly specialized market segments. According to an industry forecast by Beijing Boyan Zhishang Information Consulting Co., Ltd., the cycling equipment market in China is expected to reach 32.29 billion yuan in 2026, up 12.6 percent year-on-year. The overall cycling market is projected to surpass 60 billion yuan. Beyond traditional bicycles and accessories, technologies are opening up new space for the industry's growth. At the Tianjin Golden Wheel Bicycle Group, a smart bicycle allows its rider to connect with nearby cyclists, chat in real time and form cycling groups via a mobile application. Onboard sensors can also monitor the rider's physical conditions, while providing technical support for remote troubleshooting and maintenance. "The latest smart bicycle incorporates artificial intelligence that can learn a rider's habits and assess road conditions, making cycling easier while extending the riding range," said Li Zhenkun, marketing director of the company, which produces more than 2 million bicycles annually and exports to over 120 countries and regions. As healthier lifestyles gain currency, bicycle consumption is evolving from a functional need into a lifestyle choice, with consumers placing greater emphasis on riding experiences, product designs, smart technologies and environmental value, Li added. The boom is being fueled not only by consumer demand but also by an expanding network of cycling infrastructure. In 2024, China issued a guideline calling for stronger development of urban slow-traffic systems, including dedicated bicycle lanes. An urban renewal plan for the 2026-2030 period released in May 2026 also called for building and renovating sidewalks and non-motorized vehicle lanes to create greener urban transport systems. Cities across the country are responding by creating more cycling-friendly environments. In Shanghai, a 45-km cycling route along the Huangpu River has been formed, providing a continuous ride from the Bund to the Xuhui waterfront. In Beijing's Tongzhou District, cycling paths along the Grand Canal feature smart lighting systems and rest stops equipped with first-aid kits. Some Beijing subway lines have started letting passengers bring their bikes on board. This trial operation is making it easier for people to get where they need to go for that last stretch of their commute. These improved facilities are generating economic ripple effects that extend far beyond the bicycle industry itself. Many cities are drawing on their natural landscapes and rural resources to develop cycling routes and organize cycling events, directly stimulating demand for homestays, restaurants and rural tourism along the routes, said Wang Zongping, a professor at Nanjing University of Science and Technology. "China's rising cycling culture reflects not only a diversifying range of related businesses, but also the livability and quality of urban life, showcasing the vitality of contemporary city living," he said. ■

item.title: China pushes BeiDou navigation system deeper into global markets
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-17
CHANGSHA, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- China is advancing its BeiDou Navigation Satellite System (BDS) deeper into global markets, unveiling new products, technologies and applications at a summit in central China this week, as it seeks to position the system as a shared global service. At the 5th International Summit on BDS Applications held in Zhuzhou, Hunan Province, an international cooperation and innovation base for BeiDou applications was formally inaugurated, with plans to build a series of flagship overseas application demonstration projects and gradually construct a cooperation framework linking China's BeiDou industry with international markets. China has been steadily advancing the overseas rollout of BeiDou technology, products, standards and services, integrating the system into global infrastructure and serving economic and social development in Belt and Road countries. A report on BeiDou industry development released at the summit said that since completing global networking in 2020, the system's global service capabilities have continued to strengthen, with the foundation in place to provide stable, reliable and continuous services worldwide. BeiDou's capabilities in positioning, navigation, timing and short-message communication have continued to improve, reinforcing its global expansion in high-precision applications such as transportation, agriculture, marine fisheries and emergency rescue, according to the report. BeiDou has been fully incorporated into the standards systems of 11 international organizations, including the International Civil Aviation Organization, the International Maritime Organization and COSPAS-SARSAT, an international satellite system for search and rescue, covering core areas like civil aviation, maritime affairs and mobile communications. Zhang Junping, a Hunan provincial government official overseeing business services, said BeiDou is now one of four global satellite navigation systems recognized by the United Nations, with related products exported to more than 140 countries and regions. In Belt and Road countries, BeiDou applications and products account for 58 percent of the market, he noted. Zhang cited projects ranging from smart port operations at Peru's Chancay port to BeiDou monitoring on the China-Maldives Friendship Bridge, and from precision agriculture in Laos to taxi dispatch in Cambodia. Experts at the summit said satellite navigation is not a zero-sum game, and that BeiDou is willing to be compatible and interoperable with other global navigation systems to jointly build global spatial-temporal infrastructure. Demonstration projects have already been implemented in multiple African and Southeast Asian countries for land surveying, disaster monitoring and fisheries management. Myo Thant, deputy director general of the Myanmar Space Agency, said there is considerable potential for BeiDou applications in Myanmar, particularly in high-precision positioning, transportation, agriculture, surveying and mapping, and disaster management. "Myanmar is keen to deepen practical cooperation with China and other stakeholders in technical standards, testing and certification, professional training, capacity building, technology transfer and the development of practical BeiDou application projects," Thant added. BeiDou now provides signal coverage to over 200 countries and regions. Its international promotion is entering a key transition period from broad expansion to deeper value creation, and from product exports to ecosystem building, the report said. ■

item.title: Xi stresses sustained efforts to expand, strengthen advanced manufacturing
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-17
BEIJING, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping has urged sustained efforts to expand and strengthen advanced manufacturing to provide strong support for advancing Chinese modernization. Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks in a recent instruction, which was conveyed at a national conference on advanced manufacturing held in Beijing on Wednesday and Thursday. Efforts should be made to ensure both high-quality development and greater security, pursue smart, green and integrated development, and make the country's industrial chains more self-supporting and risk-resilient, Xi stressed. He emphasized the need to accelerate the development of a modernized industrial system with advanced manufacturing as the backbone, and reinforce the foundations of the real economy. Chinese Premier Li Qiang, also a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, delivers a speech at a national conference on advanced manufacturing held in Beijing, capital of China. The national conference on advanced manufacturing was held in Beijing on Wednesday and Thursday. An instruction of Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the CPC Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, was conveyed during the conference. (Xinhua/Huang Jingwen) Premier Li Qiang, also a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee, delivered a speech at the conference. Xi's important instructions provide essential guidance for developing advanced manufacturing, Li said, noting that China must treat developing advanced manufacturing as a major strategic task, and press steadily to boost its strength in manufacturing. Li stressed that next-generation intelligent manufacturing should serve as the primary direction, with greater emphasis on digital and intelligent empowerment, high-end manufacturing and self-reliance, green and low-carbon development, and cross-sector integration. Efforts should be made to continuously strengthen the innovation capacity, competitiveness and overall strength of advanced manufacturing, Li said. Li called for deepening the "AI plus manufacturing" initiative, stepping up guidance and support for enterprises' digital and intelligent transformation, and consolidating the foundation of intelligent software and hardware. China should also advance the deep integration of advanced manufacturing and modern services, foster service-oriented manufacturing, and cultivate advanced manufacturing clusters according to local conditions. In his concluding speech, Vice Premier Zhang Guoqing, also a member of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee, said China should further implement the initiative for high-quality development of key industrial chains, accelerate the building of a high-quality standards system, continue to address disorderly and irrational competition, and create a sound ecosystem for advanced manufacturing. ■
